items.title: Only 45 stations closed, no complete metro ban: DMRC to Supreme Court; Chairperson tenders apology
items.summary: The Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) has told the Supreme Court that there was no complete ban on metro services on the day of the proposed protests at Jantar Mantar. It said that only 45 of its 303 stations were closed for entry and exit on October 10, after the Supreme Court on October 9 ordered that there shall be no outright prohibition on the movement of metro trains. DMRC Chairperson D Thara has also tendered an "unconditional apology" in an affidavit filed in response to a contempt notice issued on October 11. On October 9, a Bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant took up an oral mentioning against Delhi Police communications. These had asked DMRC to shut entry and exit gates at 57 stations and reduce train frequency. The Court said that the notifications appeared "overreaching, as they impose a complete ban upon essential public transportation." The Bench had clarified there "shall be no outright prohibition on the movement of Metro trains". It said that any regulated arrangement should be "widely publicised". items.title: Journalist as witness to State brutality: A story from Delhi’s Pandwalan Khurd
items.summary: Delhi Police is beating protesters after detaining them. I saw this firsthand while sitting inside the blue, mesh-windowed van the police usually uses to ferry prisoners and undertrials between prisons and courts. Detained on Sunday evening (October 11), I saw three policemen pummel almost everyone who boarded after me: two stood at the van’s door at the back, and the third inside the corridor, which opened into mesh-covered, cage-like enclosures. Once each citizen entered the corridor, they were hit in the abdomen, elbowed hard in the back, kicked and worse. One youngster was pushed to the floor and beaten there. Another was viciously stamped on. These assaults were systematic, seemed to last roughly similar lengths of time for each person being detained, and served as the prologue to the shove into the cages. items.title: Emerald Heights International School moves Supreme Court seeking curbs on children's social media use
items.summary: Emerald Heights International School and its Director Siddharth Singh have moved the Supreme Court seeking restrictions on children's use of social media and an enforceable regulatory framework to protect them from online harms. The petition contends that protecting children from environments detrimental to their health, dignity and development is a constitutional responsibility of the State, and cannot be left solely to parental supervision or corporate goodwill. It has sought a direction to the Central government to frame, notify and operationalise a dedicated, comprehensive and enforceable regulatory framework to protect children on social media platforms. Alternatively, the plea seeks a prohibition on social media use by children below a prescribed age and regulation of use above that age, or enforceable age-based restrictions on children's accounts on designated platforms. The plea has invoked Article 39(f) of the Constitution, which directs the State to ensure that children develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity. Justice R Nataraj said the SLAO, who was in office when the petitioner gave his representation in 2022, shall pay the compensation within a month or the drawing officer shall deduct the same from the officer's salary. The Court said the officer harassed the senior citizen by not considering his request for referring the dispute against inadequate compensation to a court under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 from 2005. "The respondent No.2 appears to have not taken any steps to refer the dispute. This therefore shows the apparent negligence on the part of the respondent No.2 in not complying with the statutory duty prescribed under the Land Acquisition Act and also the order passed by the Additional Senior Civil Judge and JMFC, Devanahalli," the Court said. items.title: Plea filed before Karnataka High Court against conferment of 'Er' prefix for Engineers
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently sought the State's response to a writ petition challenging a State government order permitting engineers in Karnataka to prefix the honorific 'Er' before their names [ Beerappa N v State of Karnataka ]. Justice CM Poonacha issued notice in the matter on October 9. The matter will be heard next on November 16. Justice CM Poonacha The Karnataka government on September 15, 2026, issued an order that allowed engineers to attach a prefix of 'Er' before their names. A lawyer named Beerappa N has challenged the move, questioning whether the State has the authority to confer such honorifics. The petition alleges that the State provides no clear, logical explanation as to why it decided to confer an honorific on engineers, thus violating the right to equality under Article 14 of the Indian Constitution. The petition states that the State has a duty to secure a citizen's equality of status and opportunity. Conferring honorifics, on the other hand, would create a hierarchy amongst professions, the petitioner has argued. items.title: Madras HC questions Tamil Nadu police over repeated denial of RSS route marches
items.summary: The Madras High Court on Wednesday, October 14, questioned why Tamil Nadu police repeatedly denied the RSS permission for route marches despite earlier court directions. Justice V Lakshminarayanan asked why the organisation could hold marches in Jammu and Kashmir but faced repeated restrictions in Tamil Nadu. “If they (RSS) can have a march in a terrorist infested place like Jammu and Kashmir, why is the Tamil Nadu police denying permission to them every year?” the court asked, according to LiveLaw. The report said that the judge also criticised the state government for denying permission for processions organised by both the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and the Dravidar Kazhagam (DK), forcing them to approach the court. “This government is against any procession. They're denying permission for Dravidar Kazhagam and for RSS,” the court remarked. It also said the government appeared to be treating citizens as enemies by refusing permission for protests. “The government is seeing citizens as enemies.
